title: Julius Axelrod, a son of a poor Jewish neighborhood, discovered how nerves inactivate transmitters and won the Nobel Prize

trailer.text: Julius Axelrod, one of the laureates of the 1970 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, grew up in a poor Jewish neighborhood on the Lower East Side of Manhattan.
No medical school accepted him, in part because of quotas on Jews, and he began working in a laboratory for a salary of $25 a month.
In 1946 he discovered that the breakdown product of the painkiller acetanilide is itself a painkiller and does not cause methemoglobinemia, and this substance was later marketed as Tylenol.

Based on experiments, he postulated that the transmitter norepinephrine is inactivated when it is taken back up into the sympathetic nerves, and he found that tricyclic antidepressants inhibit this uptake.
For discoveries concerning the storage, release and inactivation of transmitters in the nerve terminals, he shared the Nobel Prize in 1970 with Bernard Katz and Ulf von Euler.

stations.title: A Boy from East Houston Street

paragraphs.text: Julius Axelrod was born on May 30, 1912, in New York City.
He said he was born in an apartment building on East Houston Street in Manhattan.
He grew up in a poor Jewish neighborhood on the Lower East Side.
His father made baskets and sold them to grocers in lower Manhattan from a horse and wagon.
Julius said he began working himself at 13 as a basket maker, and that he was good at it.
He also said that his real education came from the Hamilton Fish Park Library, near his home.
He began studying at New York University, but ran out of money.
He therefore transferred to the City College of New York, which charged no tuition.
At the end of his studies he tried to get into several medical schools, and was not accepted by any, in part because of quotas on Jews.
In 1970 he told a reporter that in those days it was hard for Jews to get into medical school.
In 1933, in the midst of the economic crisis, he obtained a position in a laboratory at New York University, paying $25 a month.
In 1935 he moved to the Laboratory of Industrial Hygiene, a nonprofit unit set up by the New York Health Department to test vitamin supplements.
In a laboratory accident he lost the sight in his left eye.
He said he studied for a master's degree in chemistry at New York University, in night classes.
In 1938 he married Sally Taub, and they had two children.
In his autobiography he wrote that his sons were named Paul and Alfred.
In early 1946, an institute for the study of analgesic and sedative drugs approached Axelrod's laboratory.
The institute wanted to understand why nonaspirin painkillers cause methemoglobinemia.
In their first meeting, in February 1946, Axelrod and Brodie spoke for hours about ways to solve the problem.
Axelrod developed a simple, sensitive and specific assay for aniline in urine and plasma.
Within a few weeks he discovered that the major metabolic product of acetanilide is N-acetyl-p-aminophenol.
He showed that this substance relieves pain and does not cause methemoglobinemia.
The substance, known as acetaminophen, was later marketed by the McNeil company as Tylenol.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, it became one of the best-selling painkillers in history.
Brodie and Axelrod received no royalties, because it never occurred to either of them to patent the discovery.
Brodie brought Axelrod with him to the NIH, along with other talented staff from the Goldwater laboratory.
Axelrod said that at a certain point he grew tired of working in a large team, and was allowed to work independently.
He described how, when amphetamine was given to rabbits, it disappeared without a trace, and that this is what led him to look for enzymes.
In early 1953 he demonstrated that amphetamine is degraded in liver homogenate only if cofactors such as NAD, NADP and ATP are added.
Although officially only a technician, he published the papers on the enzymes as sole author.
He considered the discovery of the microsomal enzymes to be among the best work he did.
His friends encouraged him to study for an advanced degree, but the need to support a wife and two young sons seemed to preclude it.
In 1955, at the age of 42, he received a doctorate.
Evarts offered Axelrod the opportunity to head the Section on Pharmacology, which initially consisted only of him.
Axelrod wondered whether he could find an enzyme that carries out the methylation process observed in the product VMA.
When he obtained a sample of SAM, the experiment worked excellently.
He named the enzyme catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), because the enzyme can add methyl groups to all catechols.
Measuring VMA in the urine became the standard method for diagnosing pheochromocytoma, adrenal tumors that cause hypertension.
According to Snyder, it was assumed that degradation of norepinephrine by the enzymes COMT or MAO is what inactivates it.
But inhibiting the enzymes did not end the effect of the injection.
In a decisive experiment with the visiting scientist Georg Hertting, the sympathetic nerves of a cat were lesioned, and on the lesioned side the accumulation of norepinephrine disappeared.
According to the Nobel website, in 1957 Axelrod showed how excess norepinephrine is released in response to nerve impulses and returns to its place of storage.
Axelrod discovered that cocaine, amphetamine and other sympathomimetic amines block the uptake.
He also found that major tricyclic antidepressants inhibit the uptake of norepinephrine in the heart.
Inhibition of amine uptake remains the accepted mechanism of action of these antidepressants.
The research laid the foundation for drugs such as Prozac, which selectively inhibit the reuptake of serotonin.
Reuptake of neurotransmitters is now regarded as the most frequent means of terminating synaptic transmission.
He also identified the enzyme that generates melatonin in the pineal gland.
The 1970 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Bernard Katz, Ulf von Euler and Julius Axelrod.
The prize was given for discoveries concerning the humoral transmitters in the nerve terminals and the mechanism for their storage, release and inactivation.
In a speech at the Nobel banquet, Axelrod said that their work, although fundamental, explains illnesses such as mental depression.
According to Encyclopedia.com, after the prize Axelrod made a point of crediting von Euler for the early work that led to their recognition.
Among his other honors: an honorary doctorate from the University of Chicago in 1966 and the Gairdner Foundation Award in 1967.
In 1971 he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, and in 1979 he was elected a Foreign Member of the Royal Society of London.
In 1992 he received the Ralph Gerard Prize in Neuroscience.

stations.title: A Quarter Past Eight in the Morning

paragraphs.text: According to an estimate, Axelrod mentored about 70 young scientists during his career.
Snyder described him as an ideal mentor, who taught by gradations of positive reinforcement.
According to Snyder, Axelrod arrived at the laboratory at a quarter past eight in the morning, and by half past eight he was already incubating a set of test tubes.
He said he never had any real religious feelings.
According to Encyclopedia.com, he identified with Jewish culture and joined international fights against anti-Semitism.
According to the same source, he also fought political battles on behalf of Israel.
He also opposed, in public statements, governmental attempts to focus biomedical research funding on large projects, such as finding a cure for cancer.
In 1984, at the age of 72, he formally retired from the NIMH.
In 1993 he was injected with a synthetic form of noradrenaline to raise his blood pressure before bypass surgery, a discovery to which he himself had contributed.
He died on December 29, 2004.
According to Snyder, he collapsed and died of a heart attack.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography: at his home in Rockville, Maryland
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, the work on sympathomimetic amines led to an authorship dispute between Axelrod and Brodie.
A hypothesis of Axelrod's on tolerance to narcotic drugs also stimulated considerable critical reaction, mostly negative.

claims.quote: National Academy of Sciences USA (1971) Foreign Member of the Royal Society of London (1979)

claims.text: סניידר תיאר את אקסלרוד כמנחה אידיאלי שלימד בדרך של חיזוק חיובי הדרגתי.
claims.quote: Julie was an ideal mentor, teaching by gradations of positive reinforcement.

claims.text: לפי סניידר, אקסלרוד הגיע למעבדה בשמונה ורבע בבוקר ובשמונה וחצי כבר דגר סדרת מבחנות.
claims.quote: Each day he arrived in the laboratory at 8:15 a.m. and by 8:30 was incubating a set of test tubes.

claims.text: אקסלרוד סיפר שמעולם לא היו לו רגשות דתיים אמיתיים.
claims.quote: But I never had any real religious feelings.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, אקסלרוד הזדהה עם התרבות היהודית והצטרף למאבקים בינלאומיים נגד אנטישמיות.
claims.quote: he identified with Jewish culture and joined several international fights against anti-Semitism.

claims.text: אקסלרוד נאבק פוליטית גם למען ישראל.
claims.quote: Axelrod also fought political battles on behalf of Israel.

claims.text: אקסלרוד התנגד בהצהרות פומביות לניסיונות ממשלתיים למקד את מימון המחקר הביו-רפואי בפרויקטים גדולים כמו מציאת תרופה לסרטן.
claims.quote: Axelrod repeatedly made and joined public statements against governmental attempts to target biomedical research funding to specific large-scale projects, such as finding a cure for cancer.

claims.text: ב-1984, בגיל 72, פרש רשמית מ-NIMH.
claims.quote: In 1984, at the age of 72, he formally retired from the NIMH.

claims.text: ב-1993 הוזרקה לאקסלרוד צורה סינתטית של נוראדרנלין כדי להעלות את לחץ דמו לפני ניתוח מעקפים, תגלית שהוא עצמו תרם לה.
claims.quote: However, the physicians injected a synthetic form of noradrenaline to stimulate the contractions of his heart and raise his blood pressure to an acceptable level.

claims.text: לפי סניידר, אקסלרוד התמוטט ומת מהתקף לב.
claims.quote: He had evidently arisen from bed and collapsed of a heart attack.

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, העבודה על אמינים סימפתומימטיים הובילה למחלוקת על מחברות בין אקסלרוד לברודי.
claims.quote: The work on sympathomimetic amines gave rise to an authorship dispute between Axelrod and Brodie

claims.text: ההשערה של אקסלרוד על סבילות לסמים נרקוטיים עוררה תגובה ביקורתית ניכרת, ברובה שלילית.
claims.quote: This hypothesis stimulated considerable critical reaction, mostly negative.

claims.text: בנוסח של סניידר בגרסה אחרת, המעבר לקולג' העירוני התרחש ב-1936.
claims.quote: Julie began college at New York University but ran out of money and transferred in 1936 to the City College of New York, which was tuition-free.

claims.text: לפי הביוגרפיה של פרס נובל, התואר השני התקבל ב-1941 והדוקטורט ב-1955.
claims.quote: M. A. in 1941 at New York University, and Ph. D. in 1955 from the George Washington University.

claims.text: אקסלרוד סיפר בראיון שאחד מילדיו נולד ב-1945 והשני ב-1949.
claims.quote: One was born in 1945, and the other was born in 1949.

claims.text: לפי סניידר, אקסלרוד שוחח עם פול ק. סמית', ראש הפרמקולוגיה באוניברסיטת ג'ורג' וושינגטון, בעניין הדוקטורט.
claims.quote: Finally, Julie spoke with Paul K. Smith, chair of pharmacology at George Washington University

claims.text: לפי הספרייה הלאומית לרפואה, המנחה שלו בדוקטורט היה ג'ורג' מנדל, שאיפשר לו להגיש עבודה מה-NIH כבסיס לדיסרטציה.
claims.quote: where his advisor, George Mandel, permitted him to submit some of his recent NIH laboratory work as the basis of his doctoral dissertation.

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, אקסלרוד מת בביתו ברוקוויל, מרילנד.
claims.quote: Axelrod reportedly died in his sleep at his home in Rockville, Maryland.

claims.text: המחקר הניח את היסוד לתרופות כמו פרוזק, שמעכבות באופן סלקטיבי ספיגה חוזרת של סרוטונין.
claims.quote: work by blocking the reuptake process that Axelrod identified

claims.text: ב-1992 קיבל את פרס ראלף ג'ראר במדעי המוח.
claims.quote: 1992: Julius Axelrod, PhD

claims.text: הוא מת ב-29 בדצמבר 2004.
claims.quote: died on December 29, 2004, at his home in Rockville, Md.
